title: Graduated slowdown protocol and post-incident notes
content:
Summary:

This note captures the event on 2026-02-03 where a set of compromised API keys produced a sustained high QPS for ~6 hours and triggered cascading quota exhaustions in a few customer routes. Instead of immediate hard-blocking, we experimented with a graduated slowdown (soft-throttles, response-chunk pacing, and increasing error bias) to preserve availability for legitimate traffic and reduce blast radius. This doc records the timeline, signal logic used, operator steps taken, observed impact, and a proposed trimmed-down runbook for oncall teams.

Why we tried graduated slowdown:
- Past hard-blocks caused severe user-visible failures and escalations for impacted customers (see incident log JIRA-5401).
- The attack pattern was volumetric but had a high degree of repetition in user-agent + header fingerprint, so we could apply heuristics without full customer-wide blocks.
- We wanted to validate whether soft measures could reduce tokens served while giving customers time to rotate keys.

High level outcome:
- Traffic dropped from a peak of ~1.9M requests/min to ~220k req/min after the full policy stack was applied over 27 minutes.
- Token spend reduced ~86% for affected routes, queue latencies improved but tail latency still spiked for some small customers.
- No customer SLA breach escalations received during the incident window — largely due to early downstream rate-limiting on per-customer routes.

Timeline (concise):
- 2026-02-03 03:14 UTC — Alert: anomaly_detector -> route-generation-time-series high QPS for /v1/generate-chat (signal id: AD-2041).
- 03:17 UTC — Oncall (Aisha) verifies traffic shape: stealthy repeated calls from ~420 distinct API keys, identical prompt sizes, similar IP prefixes (cloud provider proxies).
- 03:22 UTC — Quick mitigation: enable per-key soft token cap (slow-path) and deploy temporary KV-cache bypass for these keys to avoid cache poisoning side-effects.
- 03:30 UTC — Graduated slowdown policy rolled: 1) 20% request drop (probabilistic), 2) 50ms enforced response-chunk delay, 3) priority demotion to background queue.
- 03:41 UTC — WAF rules tuned to treat the fingerprint as suspicious (added signature but kept tiered, not global block).
- 04:01 UTC — Metrics show QPS at ~420k; token rate down 70%.
- 04:39 UTC — Customers with heavy usage contacted via automated notify (ops-notify) with remediation guidance and rotation instructions.
- 09:40 UTC — Gradual relaxation to normal policies after keys rotated or failed auth for ~80% of the initial bad keys.

Signals used to decide escalation level:
- per-key token issuance rate > 300 tokens/s sustained for 2min
- repeated identical prompt hashes across >50 requests in 5s windows
- new key seen with no previous activity hitting >200 QPS within first 10 minutes of issuance
- IP / ASN clusters with >95% requests flagged by threat intel feed
- sudden drop in KV cache hit ratio accompanied by rising tail latency

Operator playbook (draft checklist for oncall):
1) Confirm signal: open dashboards (ops/generate-qps, ops/token-rate, ops/cache-hits) and capture the time series snapshot.
2) Identify candidate keys: run key-fingerprint query (internal quick script: infra/scripts/key_fingerprint.sh --window=10m).
3) Apply graduated slowdown (preferred order):
   a) Probabilistic dropper (start 20% -> increase to 60% if no improvement)
   b) Insert fixed inter-chunk delay for streaming routes (+50ms -> +250ms if needed)
   c) Drop to low-priority queue (background processing) for non-paying tiers
   d) Soft 429 with X-Backoff header (gives clients clear rotation hint)
4) Add temporary WAF signature in monitor mode first. If fingerprints match and false-positive risk low, escalate to enforced block for that signature only.
5) Notify customers: use ops-notify automated template; escalate to SE/CS when customer is enterprise or shows/responds poorly.
6) Rotate compromised keys if we control distribution (internal test keys); request customers rotate via API key rotation endpoint.
7) If abuse persists or cross-customer impact increases, move to credential-level hard-block and key invalidation.

Commands and quick queries (operators):
- List hot keys: curl -sS "https://ops-api.local/hot-keys?window=10m" | jq .
- Kill temporary token issuance for key X: post /admin/keys/X/soft-throttle
- Set probabilistic drop for route: POST /ops/policies --body '{"route":"/v1/generate-chat","drop":0.2,"duration":"10m"}'
- Add WAF rule in monitor mode: wafctl create --expr "ua_fingerprint:..." --mode monitor

Observed failure modes and lessons learned:
- False positives on shared library clients: two legitimate SDKs route through similar proxies and matched the fingerprint leading to customer confusion. Mitigation: pair fingerprint with prompt-hash and per-key history before hard action.
- Cache invalidation side-effects: temporary bypass for suspected keys prevented cache poisoning but caused a small spike in downstream compute. Add capacity headroom step in future.
- Long delay in customer rotation: some customers did not rotate quickly; we lacked a firm escalation hook to forcibly expire keys for enterprise accounts without legal/CS approval. Need pre-approved escalation policy.

Runbook insert (proposed short form — cut & paste friendly):
- When token_rate_per_key > 300 t/s for 2m AND identical_prompt_share > 20%:
  1) Set policy: probabilistic_drop=0.2 duration=15m
  2) Add response_chunk_delay=50ms for streaming routes
  3) Mark keys in dashboard tag "suspected-abuse" and call ops-notify template
  4) If no improvement in 15m: increase drop to 0.5 and notify SRE lead
  5) After 30m if still high: escalate to hard block and open JIRA incident (use template JIRA-ABUSE-CRIT)

Follow-ups and action items (owners):
- Marcus Chen: build a safer fingerprinting pipeline that requires at least 2 independent signals before a rule flips to enforced (due 2026-03-01).
- Elena García: author customer rotation playbook and add an automated enterprise expiry flow for repeated abuse (due 2026-03-08).
- Samir Rao: add graduated slowdown knobs to the console UI for SRE/CS operators (UX sketch due 2026-02-28).
- Aisha Patel (me): consolidate metrics dashboard panels and add a single-click "apply graduated slowdown" button in the ops portal (proof of concept by 2026-03-05).

Open questions for follow-up discussions:
- What is an acceptable false-positive rate for WAF enforce actions at scale?
- Should the platform offer a customer-facing UI to self-rotate keys triggered by detected abuse (pros/cons)?
- How do we bill/credit customers for tokens misused by compromised keys during an abuse event?

Appendix: quick incident notes (raw timeline snippets) and Slack references:
- Slack: #sre-oncall thread (message ids: p2345abcd)
- Raw graphs stored: s3://ops-metrics/incident-2026-02-03/
- Commands executed (history): /admin/policies applied: probabilistic_drop=0.2 -> 03:30 UTC; response_chunk_delay=50ms -> 03:32 UTC; waf rule monitor -> 03:41 UTC

End notes:
This incident validated that graduated slowdown is a useful escape hatch to preserve overall platform availability while we remediate leaks and notify customers. The main risks are false-positive customer impact and complexity of orchestration across rate-limit layers. Next steps are to wire safer fingerprint gating, improve customer communication flows, and add operator tooling to reduce manual steps.
